content: Leadership Dynamics, also referred to as the Leadership Dynamics Institute (LDI), was a private, for-profit organization founded and owned by William Penn Patrick. The company specialized in executive training, personal development, and self-improvement programs. It is recognized as the first example of what psychologists later termed Large Group Awareness Training. In 1967, William Penn Patrick authored a booklet titled Happiness and Success through Principle and subsequently established Leadership Dynamics based on the principles outlined in the booklet. Employees in management positions at Holiday Magic, another company associated with Patrick, were required to participate in Leadership Dynamics courses. These courses were described as incorporating elements reminiscent of strict military training techniques. Patrick not only provided financial support for Leadership Dynamics but also funded Holiday Magic and Alexander Everett's Mind Dynamics. He claimed that participants in Leadership Dynamics programs would be equipped to lead more creative and constructive lives. The principles of Everett's Mind Dynamics were integrated into the Leadership Dynamics curriculum. Ben Gay, a senior instructor at Leadership Dynamics, also served as the President of Holiday Magic in the United States. Although Gay asserted that Leadership Dynamics was an entirely separate entity from Holiday Magic, author Gene Church highlighted numerous inconsistencies in this claim. According to a lawsuit filed by the Securities and Exchange Commission against Holiday Magic, employees were required to complete Leadership Dynamics training to advance to higher-ranking positions such as Instructor General, Trainer General, and Senior General. In 1970, Patrick acquired Mind Dynamics, and the Leadership Dynamics courses gained popularity in the United States, Europe, and Australia. Michael Langone, writing in Business and Society Review, identified Leadership Dynamics as one of the earliest examples of transformational training. The company’s extreme approach to human potential movement training resulted in numerous lawsuits. Participants in the courses were reportedly subjected to abusive practices, including physical beatings, food and sleep deprivation, confinement in coffins, and degrading sexual acts. Former participants alleged in lawsuits that they were sexually abused and tortured during the training sessions. Specific accounts described individuals being placed in coffins or on crosses. Navarro and Navarro characterized the training as employing a harsh and hard-hitting style of group encounter therapy. These practices were detailed in the non-fiction book The Pit: A Group Encounter Defiled, which was later adapted into the film Circle of Power. Navarro and Navarro also noted that Werner Erhard adopted the confrontational and abusive group encounter techniques of Leadership Dynamics to develop Erhard Seminars Training (EST). Langone observed that many subsequent forms of transformational training were, at the very least, indirectly influenced by Leadership Dynamics. John Hanley, the founder of Lifespring, attended a Leadership Dynamics course while working for Holiday Magic. Chris Mathe, a clinical psychology Ph.D. candidate at the time, wrote that most modern forms of Large Group Awareness Training were modeled after the Leadership Dynamics Institute. Mathe specifically identified groups such as Erhard Seminars Training, Landmark Education, Lifespring, Insight Seminars, New Warriors, and Impact as being influenced by Leadership Dynamics.
